do: Let buttons hug their label plus fixed padding, fixing only the dimension that must stay constant (such as height).
Use flex or grid gaps for lists and cards so repeated items keep consistent spacing.
Use full width only where the layout calls for it, such as a bottom action on mobile.
avoid: Fixed button widths that clip longer labels, or absolute positioning that breaks when content changes.

rules.title: Same look, same meaning
rules.why: Elements that look alike are read as related, so visual treatments must map consistently to meaning.
do: Style every element with the same function identically: one button style per emphasis level, one link color, one chip shape.
Use one shared component for parallel items such as pricing tiers, and emphasize the recommended one with a single deliberate variant.
Group items that share a state together (for example unread items first).
avoid: Reusing a highlight style for unrelated purposes, or letting heading and icon colors drift between sibling cards.

rules.title: Give segmented controls an inset track
rules.why: An inset track makes segmented options read as one control.
do: Wrap the options in a track with about 4-8px inset, and show the selected option as a raised or contrasting pill.
Give each option button-like padding and keyboard support.
avoid: Segmented options placed directly on the page background with no track.

rules.title: Keep tooltips short and reachable without hover
rules.why: Brief contextual help explains a control without cluttering the layout, but hover-only help excludes touch and keyboard users.
do: Show tooltips on hover, keyboard focus and tap, anchored to the trigger, with one or two short sentences or a 1-4 word label.
Give icon buttons an aria-label matching their tooltip, and give first-run hints an explicit "Got it".
avoid: Essential instructions that exist only in a tooltip, or interactive content inside tooltips.

rules.title: Use modals for focused tasks and popovers for light context
rules.why: Blocking overlays interrupt; they should be reserved for tasks that need full attention.
do: Use a modal (scrim, trapped focus, visible close, Escape to dismiss, Cancel plus one primary action) for focused edits.
Use a non-blocking popover anchored to its trigger for short contextual content, dismissed by an outside click or Escape.
Return focus to the trigger when either closes.
avoid: Blocking overlays for trivial information, or dialogs with no visible way out.

rules.title: Give avatars fixed sizes and fallbacks
rules.why: Avatars personalize the interface, but missing photos must never break the layout.
do: Use a fixed size scale (for example 24, 32, 40, 48, 64px).
Fall back from photo to initials to a generic person icon, and place status badges at the bottom-right, scaled with the avatar.
Add a 2-4px ring in the surface color when an avatar overlaps a photo or another avatar.
avoid: Broken-image icons or arbitrary avatar sizes per screen.

rules.title: Structure action menus
rules.why: Account and overflow menus stay scannable when items are grouped and the exit action is isolated.
do: Open with a header that identifies the context (avatar, name), then group related items with dividers and leading icons.
Show shortcut hints right-aligned on desktop, and place Sign out or destructive items last in their own group.
avoid: A long undivided list, or Sign out mixed into everyday items.

rules.title: Make cards self-contained modules
rules.why: One topic per bounded card makes feeds and dashboards scannable and lets them reflow responsively.
do: Give each card one topic: a title, one key value, supporting metadata and at most one or two actions.
Keep padding, radius and separation identical across sibling cards.
avoid: Unrelated data or several competing buttons in one card.

rules.title: Make selected items obvious
rules.why: A small checked box alone is easy to miss in a list.
do: Change the whole row when selected (accent fill or tint, stronger border) and keep a check or checkbox as a non-color cue.
avoid: A selected row that looks identical to unselected ones except for a tiny checkbox.

rules.title: Give KPI tiles a fixed anatomy
rules.why: Dashboards are scanned tile by tile; a fixed structure makes every number interpretable at a glance.
do: Order each tile as a small label, a large value with tabular numerals, then a delta with arrow, sign and comparison period ("+4.9% vs last month"), with an optional icon or sparkline.
Render tiles from a data array of raw values mapped to one component, formatting with Intl.NumberFormat at render time.
Add a hover lift only when the tile opens a detail view, and give it a focus style too.
avoid: Up or down shown by green and red alone, hover lift on non-interactive tiles, or preformatted strings that cannot be sorted.

rules.title: Make charts answer one question and reveal exact values
rules.why: A chart is only useful if the reader knows what it shows, over what period, and can read exact values.
do: Give each chart a title, a one-line summary, a time-range control and labeled axes, and highlight the current or key series while muting the rest.
Show exact values in tooltips on hover and keyboard focus, put the total in the center of donuts, and list values beside legend entries.
Provide a text or table alternative and wrap charts in a responsive container.
avoid: Color-only legends, tiny low-contrast axis labels, glossy or 3D bars that distort comparison, or entrance animations replayed on every refresh.

rules.title: Build operational tables for triage
rules.why: Lists are read by status and recency; those must be scannable without decoding.
do: Use real table markup with th scope="col", right-aligned numbers with tabular numerals, and status pills with words.
Add filter tabs with counts above the table, show relative times with the absolute timestamp in a time element, and highlight the selected row with aria-selected beside a detail pane.
avoid: Column widths that jump when the selection changes, or status shown by a colored dot alone.

rules.title: Give list rows a leading visual, two lines and a trailing value
rules.why: A consistent row anatomy makes transactions, devices and people lists scannable.
do: Place an avatar, logo or icon first, primary text above secondary text, and the key value right-aligned at the end.
Keep signs on money values (-$24.00, +$240.00) with tabular numerals, group long lists under date headers, and keep tappable rows at least 48px tall.
avoid: Red and green as the only difference between debits and credits, or truncated trailing values.

rules.title: Keep product cards comparable
rules.why: Uniform cards let shoppers compare quickly across a grid.
do: Use a fixed image aspect-ratio with object-fit: cover, then category, name, price (right-aligned or accent), rating with its count, and one add action with an accessible name that includes the product.
Make the title the card's link and keep the add button outside the link; use grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(220px, 1fr)) for the grid.
avoid: Price or the add action shown only on hover, varying image heights, or nested interactive elements.

rules.title: Give carousels controls, position and a pause
rules.why: Rotating content hides information, so people need control over it.
do: Provide labeled previous and next buttons, a position indicator ("3 of 8"), keyboard arrows and scroll snapping.
Pause on hover and focus and offer a pause control if anything autoplays; treat 3D coverflow as optional styling over the same controls.
avoid: Autoplay without a way to stop it, drag as the only way to move, or the only copy of critical information inside a carousel.

rules.title: Give segmented controls and chips real selection semantics
rules.why: Compact toggles are fast, but assistive technology must know what is selected.
do: Use native radios or role="radiogroup" with role="radio" and aria-checked for single choice, and toggle buttons with aria-pressed or checkboxes for multi-select chips.
Move selection with arrow keys using a roving tabindex, and show the selected state with fill plus a check or weight change.
Let horizontal chip rows scroll with the last chip peeking past the edge.
avoid: ARIA roles without the matching keyboard behavior, or a faint tint as the only selected cue.

rules.title: Make swatch pickers named radio groups
rules.why: Swatches are single-choice inputs and must be operable and named like one.
do: Build them as a radio group, give each swatch a text name, and mark the selected one with an offset ring plus the visible variant name.
Keep the hit area at least 44px even when the visible dot is small, and update an accent token so the whole product view reflects the choice.
avoid: Unnamed color dots, or a per-variant accent that fails contrast on its background.

rules.title: Keep the current selection visible and removable
rules.why: People should always see what they picked and be able to undo it without reopening a menu.
do: Show the selected value in the trigger, or as a chip with a labeled remove button.
Announce changes in a polite live region and use listbox or menu semantics with Escape returning focus to the trigger.
avoid: Replacing the labeled trigger with an unlabeled icon once a value is chosen.

rules.title: Route accents through one token per theme or variant
rules.why: When every accent use reads one custom property, re-theming and per-item colors stay consistent.
do: Define the accent once (for example --accent) and set it per theme or variant with a data attribute, using it for text, fills, borders, glows and focus.
Check each variant's accent against its own background.
avoid: Repeating accent hex values across many rules.

rules.title: Use a large fixed radius for pills
rules.why: A fixed large radius keeps semicircular ends at any width, while 50% turns wide elements into ellipses.
do: Use border-radius: 999px for pills, chips, pill buttons and indicators.
avoid: border-radius: 50% on non-square elements.

rules.title: Prefer the native share sheet
rules.why: The system share sheet lists the user's own apps; a custom icon row is only a fallback.
do: Call navigator.share when navigator.canShare allows it, and otherwise expand a row of labeled share targets plus "Copy link" with immediate confirmation.
avoid: Unlabeled brand icons, or a share row that opens on hover.

rules.title: Give feeds and notifications a fixed item anatomy
rules.why: A predictable order makes long feeds and notification lists scannable.
do: Show avatar, name, relative time and an overflow menu with an accessible name, then body text clamped to 2-3 lines with an in-place "See more", then media and reactions with counts.
For notifications, put the actor in bold, the action text and a relative time, entering with a short slide and fade.
avoid: Wrapping a card that contains buttons in one big link, or autoplaying video with sound.

rules.title: Lay out media players in the familiar order
rules.why: Familiar control order lets people operate a player without hunting.
do: Show artwork, title and artist, a progress bar with elapsed and total time, then shuffle, previous, a larger play or pause, next and repeat.
Give icon buttons accessible names and reflect toggles such as shuffle and repeat with aria-pressed.
avoid: A play button the same size and weight as the secondary controls.

rules.title: Build checklists from real checkboxes with a live count
rules.why: Clear done states and a running tally give a sense of progress.
do: Use labeled checkboxes, show done items with a check, line-through and reduced emphasis, and update "3 of 8 completed" in a polite live region.
Name delete buttons after their item and offer undo.
avoid: Deleting with no undo, or low-contrast placeholder text on dark surfaces.

rules.title: Lay out receipts and money summaries for checking
rules.why: Financial summaries must be easy to verify line by line.
do: Use label and value rows with tabular numerals and right-aligned amounts, listing subtotal, discount (with a minus sign), fees, tax with its rate and a bold total, plus a reference number.
Render receipts as real text that can be selected, printed or downloaded.
avoid: Marking discounts by red alone, or decoration that covers the figures.

rules.title: Use one icon family and one style
rules.why: Mixed icon styles look assembled from scraps and can make one icon seem selected.
do: Use a single icon library with one style (outline or filled), one stroke width and one size grid (for example 20 or 24px), optically centered.
If filled icons mean "active", apply that rule to every item.
avoid: Filled and outline icons, or different stroke widths, in the same bar or list.

rules.title: Use conventional icon metaphors
rules.why: Familiar icons are recognized instantly; novel metaphors make users guess.
do: Use widely understood icons: gear for settings, sliders for filters, bookmark for save-for-later, paper plane for send, lock for privacy, globe for language.
Add a text label wherever an icon could be ambiguous.
avoid: Custom metaphors for common actions, or an icon that conventionally means something else.

rules.title: Add leading icons to list and settings rows
rules.why: A familiar icon beside each label is a second cue that makes long lists faster to scan.
do: Place a 20-24px icon at the start of each row in a single aligned column.
Keep the text label and mark decorative icons aria-hidden.
avoid: Long text-only settings lists, or icons that replace the label.

rules.title: Give icon-only controls a name
rules.why: Screen readers and new users cannot interpret an unlabeled glyph.
do: Give every icon-only control an aria-label and a tooltip with the same text.
Prefer visible labels for primary navigation and uncommon actions.
avoid: Unnamed icon buttons, or names that differ from the visible tooltip.

rules.title: Use imagery that supports the message
rules.why: Images that do not illustrate the message add noise; relevant visuals speed understanding.
do: Choose images or illustrations that show what the headline promises, in a style consistent with the brand.
Keep content backgrounds calm and let product imagery provide the visual interest.
avoid: Generic stock photos as filler, or decorative blobs and shapes behind product grids and text.

rules.title: Crop images to keep the subject visible
rules.why: Cropping that cuts off the subject makes a card lose its meaning.
do: Use object-fit: cover with object-position set to the subject's focal point, and check crops at each breakpoint.
avoid: Stretched images (object-fit: fill) or automatic center crops that cut off faces or products.

rules.title: Normalize SVG strokes for progress and scaling
rules.why: A few SVG attributes keep line weights stable when graphics scale and make progress strokes trivial to drive.
do: Set pathLength="1" and drive stroke-dasharray and stroke-dashoffset in 0-1 units for rings, borders and draw-on lines.
Add vector-effect="non-scaling-stroke" to strokes in responsively scaled SVGs, and transform-box: fill-box on parts that rotate or scale around their own center.
Start rings at 12 o'clock with a -90 degree rotation and round line caps.
avoid: Calling getTotalLength every frame, or a solid spinning ring for something that is not loading.

rules.title: Switch from outline to filled for hover and active icons
rules.why: Swapping an outline icon for its filled version is a clear, low-cost state change.
do: Use outline icons at rest and filled or tinted versions for hover, selected and :focus-visible, with the label weight increased.
Transition only the properties that change (color, opacity, transform) for about 200-300ms.
avoid: transition: all, or hover animation as the only sign of interactivity on touch devices.

rules.title: Ship a still fallback for animated illustrations
rules.why: Animated illustrations can fail to load or need pausing; a still frame keeps the page meaningful.
do: Include a static image of the key frame alongside any Lottie or canvas animation, with the alt text on one of them and the other aria-hidden.
Show the still when scripts fail or prefers-reduced-motion is set.
avoid: An empty box until the animation library loads.

rules.title: Generate repeated SVG parts in code
rules.why: Radial or repeated details are easier to tune when generated in a loop than drawn by hand.
do: Create nodes with document.createElementNS("http://www.w3.org/2000/svg", "rect"), rotate each by i * 360 / count, build once, then animate the group with one transform.
Draw evenly spaced ticks with one circle and a dash pattern where possible.
avoid: document.createElement for SVG elements (they land in the HTML namespace and do not render), or one DOM node per tick when a dash pattern would do.

rules.title: Keep pixel art crisp
rules.why: Default smoothing blurs pixel art and bitmap-style lettering.
do: Set image-rendering: pixelated on scaled sprites and canvases and scale by whole-number factors.
avoid: Fractional scaling of pixel assets, or pixel fonts for body text.

rules.title: Label buttons with the outcome
rules.why: A verb that names the result tells users exactly what will happen.
do: Use verb plus object: "Save changes", "Add to basket", "Delete project", "Pay $12.96".
Keep the label consistent with the screen title and the confirmation message.
avoid: "Yes", "No", "OK", "Submit" or "Done" when a specific verb exists, or a bare noun as a label.

rules.title: Keep button labels on one line
rules.why: Wrapped button text looks broken and gets worse on small screens and in translation.
do: Write labels of 1-3 words and test at the narrowest supported width (320px) and in long languages.
Shorten the copy or let the button go full width instead of wrapping.
avoid: Labels that break onto two lines, or shrinking the font below the standard button size.

rules.title: Write labels in plain language
rules.why: Internal or marketing jargon confuses users who have never seen those terms.
do: Name settings by their effect ("Hide balances", "Help and support"), and be specific with legal links ("Privacy policy", "Terms and conditions").
Use standard wording for account actions: "Log out", "Close account".
Phrase toggle labels as the state that turning them on produces.
avoid: Team-internal feature names, single vague nouns, or the same word for two different rows.

rules.title: Keep confirmations short
rules.why: People skim, so brief messages are understood faster.
do: Use one or two words for routine confirmations ("Saved", "Copied") next to the relevant icon.
Add detail only when users need it to decide or act.
avoid: Full exclamatory sentences for simple confirmations.

rules.title: Ship no placeholder copy
rules.why: Leftover template words are the first thing users notice and they undermine trust.
do: Search the UI and code for "Title", "Button", "Label", "Text", "Lorem ipsum" and similar strings before shipping.
Use realistic sample data in demos and empty fixtures.
avoid: A checkout card headed "Title" with a button labeled "Button".

rules.title: Avoid all-caps labels
rules.why: Mixed case keeps word shapes recognizable, so it reads faster and feels calmer.
do: Write labels in sentence case or title case and apply one convention across the product.
Keep source strings in natural case and set text-transform: none on buttons.
avoid: All-caps primary buttons or long all-caps labels.

rules.title: Say where the code went and when it can be resent
rules.why: Naming the destination and the wait prevents duplicate requests and doubt about the address used.
do: State the code length and the masked destination ("4-digit code sent to ••• 0142") with a link to change it.
Keep "Resend" visibly disabled during a cooldown with a live label ("Resend in 0:24") and enable it at zero.
Announce only when resend becomes available, not every second.
avoid: Hiding the resend option until the timer ends, or styling enabled and disabled resend identically.

rules.title: Format numbers with one locale everywhere
rules.why: Mixed separators make amounts ambiguous (99.560 next to 14,867).
do: Format every number and currency through Intl.NumberFormat with one locale, including chart axes, tooltips and tables.
Use compact notation ("$164.4K") for axis ticks and donut centers and full precision in tooltips and details.
avoid: Hand-built number strings, mixed decimal marks, or currency symbols on some values but not others.

rules.title: After success, relabel with the outcome or the next step
rules.why: A button that still says "Send" after sending invites a second click.
do: Switch to a past-tense confirmation ("Sent", "Added", "Downloaded") with a check, or to the obvious next action ("Open file").
Make the confirmation visually quieter than the original call to action.
avoid: Leaving the original verb in place after success.

rules.title: Translate raw numbers into consequences
rules.why: People act on outcomes ("safe for 2 hours") more than on units ("88 dB").
do: Pair a technical value with a plain-language consequence and a status word (Quiet, Loud, Danger), computed from a documented model.
avoid: The raw number alone, or alarmist copy the model does not support.

rules.title: State offer conditions up front
rules.why: Deals feel trustworthy when dates and limits are visible before the click.
do: Show the discount with a one-line benefit, its validity dates or channel limits, and a link to the terms.
Show the original price struck through (s or del) beside the new one and the saving.
avoid: Conditions hidden in fine print after the click, or "limited time" claims that keep reappearing.

rules.title: Make trust and data-safety statements specific
rules.why: In finance and data products, concrete statements about access and control build trust before people connect accounts.
do: Use a few short cards, each with an icon, a 2-3 word title and one specific sentence (for example read-only access, encrypted connections, how to disconnect).
Place them next to the step that asks for access.
avoid: Vague security claims, or low-contrast gray body text in those cards.

rules.title: Show ratings with their scale and sample size
rules.why: A bare star count is not believable; scale and count are.
do: Show the rating with its scale (4.9/5) and a real count of reviews or users, and link to the reviews.
avoid: Ratings with no scale or count, or invented figures.

rules.title: Explain unusual interactions in two or three words
rules.why: When a control is not a standard button, a tiny instruction prevents confusion.
do: Place a short, quiet instruction beside the affordance ("Pull and release", "Hold to confirm") and provide a click or keyboard alternative.
avoid: Relying on users to discover a gesture with no hint.

rules.title: Offer fewer, clearer choices
rules.why: Decision time grows with the number and similarity of options.
do: Show only the options most users need at each step and move the rest behind "More" or "Advanced".
Mark a recommended default and give options short distinguishing subtitles.
Collapse fine-grained ranges into a few non-overlapping buckets (for example 0-1, 2-3, 4-5, 6+).
avoid: Long flat lists of near-identical options, or every setting on the first screen.

rules.title: Put key items first and last
rules.why: People remember the first and last items of a sequence best; the middle is the weakest spot.
do: Lead lists, onboarding and landing sections with the strongest benefit or most-used item.
Place the most important action at the end of a sequence.
avoid: Burying essential information or actions in the middle of a long list.

rules.title: Chunk information without hard caps
rules.why: Grouped information is easier to scan and remember than one undivided mass.
do: Group related items under headings or spacing, keeping each visible group small.
Format long values in chunks (card numbers 4-4-4-4, phone numbers by local convention).
Reveal further items on demand.
avoid: Sixteen or more equally weighted items in one grid with no grouping.
rules.note: The "seven plus or minus two" figure describes short-term recall, not a hard limit on menu or navigation length.

rules.title: Prefer conventions over trends
rules.why: Trendy effects date quickly and often add noise; standard patterns stay clear and familiar.
do: Default to solid single-color primary buttons, standard navigation placement and platform conventions.
Express personality through one or two restrained touches such as an accent color or illustration.
avoid: Multi-color gradient buttons or extra floating controls added only for flair.

rules.title: Polish shapes perceived usability
rules.why: People perceive well-crafted interfaces as easier to use and forgive small issues in them.
do: Keep typography, spacing, color and corner radius consistent and deliberate on every screen.
Still test the flow itself, because polish can hide real usability problems.
avoid: Treating visual consistency as optional or "later".

rules.title: Give enough detail; avoid over-minimal UI
rules.why: Stripping supporting details in the name of minimalism leaves users guessing about state and size.
do: Show useful metadata under item titles (file size, date, episode number).
Label progress bars with a value and give in-progress tasks a cancel control.
Label ambiguous numbers ("Episode 3", not "#3").
avoid: Removing information that helps users decide.

rules.title: Build dashboards around the decision they support
rules.why: Every widget should help users understand or act; decorative or redundant widgets bury the key numbers.
do: Lead with one primary metric and its trend, with a period selector.
Follow with 3-4 secondary KPI cards showing value and change, then a short recent-items table with status pills and "View all".
Show the primary value large and the raw numbers smaller and muted.
avoid: Ten or more small widgets, upsell cards and icon grids on one screen, or uniform "Label: value" lists with equal weight.

rules.title: Show statuses as labeled pills
rules.why: Status written as small plain text blends into metadata; colored pills are scannable.
do: Render statuses as small pill badges with a consistent color per status, keeping the status word inside the pill.
Check the text contrast against the pill fill.
avoid: Status as faint gray text styled like other metadata, or color without a label.

rules.title: Group settings into titled sections
rules.why: A long flat list makes people read every row; themed groups let them jump to the right cluster.
do: Split settings into groups such as Security, General and Legal, each with a small muted label and its own inset block.
Put session and destructive actions ("Log out", "Close account") in a separate final group.
avoid: Twelve or more unrelated rows in one list, or destructive actions mixed with everyday preferences.

rules.title: Disclose settings progressively
rules.why: Showing the most-used options first reduces load while details stay one tap away.
do: Keep frequent settings at the top level and move detailed options into sub-pages opened from chevron rows.
Add quick actions on detail pages, such as a copy button beside each account value.
avoid: Every option on one screen, or common actions buried several levels deep.

rules.title: Add search to long settings
rules.why: Typing a keyword is faster than drilling in and out of sub-screens.
do: Add a search field under the settings title once the list grows past about 6-8 items.
Match labels, section names and common synonyms, and show each result with its group.
avoid: Forcing users to browse nested screens to find one option.

rules.title: Personalize the account header
rules.why: Showing the user's name and avatar makes the account area feel personal and confirms the right account.
do: Title the account screen with the user's name and plan, with an avatar, initials fallback and an edit badge.
Keep any offer card secondary and dismissible.
avoid: Turning the account screen into an ad surface.

rules.title: Make search one prominent field with filters on demand
rules.why: Most people just want to type; a wall of filters up front slows everyone down.
do: Use one full-width input with a magnifier icon and a specific placeholder ("Search products").
Put advanced filters behind a single filter button or panel, submit on Enter and show a clear control only after text is entered.
avoid: Five or more dropdowns plus extra buttons before anything is typed, or vague placeholders like "Type here".

rules.title: Collect sensible defaults during onboarding
rules.why: Gathering key preferences early lets the product start personal instead of blank.
do: Ask one topic per screen with a progress bar and a single Continue button.
Reuse the answers to prefill the profile and settings, keeping every value editable, and flag anything unconfirmed inline.
avoid: Asking again later for information already collected.

rules.title: Keep preference setup skippable
rules.why: A short preference step personalizes the experience, but forcing it traps users.
do: Offer a visible Skip with sensible defaults, and let users change preferences later in settings.
avoid: Mandatory wizards, or asking for preferences the product does not use.

rules.title: Open with a clear welcome screen
rules.why: The first screen sets expectations and trust.
do: Pair one relevant visual with a short value headline.
Offer a filled "Get started" and a lower-emphasis "Log in", with page dots if it is a short carousel.
avoid: A bare login form with no context, or a long animated splash screen.

rules.title: Keep hero sections focused
rules.why: One message, one action and one trust signal communicate value within seconds.
do: Use a top bar with the logo left, a few short links and one distinct action on the right.
Use one headline of a few short lines, one supporting sentence, one primary call to action and a trust signal such as a rating or outcome figure.
Pair the text with one dominant visual, keep text on calm image areas, and stack headline above the action on mobile.
avoid: Several equally weighted calls to action, long navigation menus, or competing badges and decorations.

rules.title: Lay out sign-in screens predictably
rules.why: A familiar sign-in layout lets people and password managers finish quickly.
do: Order the card as heading and one-line subtitle, fields, "remember me" with its duration beside "Forgot password?", full-width primary button, an "or continue with" divider, equal-width provider buttons, then a sign-up link.
On desktop, cap the form column at about 360-420px beside an optional visual panel; on mobile show the form first.
Keep the same shell for follow-up steps (code entry, password reset) so the flow feels continuous.
avoid: Essential copy only in a decorative panel that disappears on mobile, or looping animation beside the form.

rules.title: Never gate a core task behind a playful interaction
rules.why: People who came to sign in or pay should not have to discover a gesture or wait for a character first.
do: Render the form or main action on load, and let any playful element run alongside it as optional decoration.
If a reveal interaction is kept, also offer a visible, keyboard-operable button and a skip.
avoid: Hiding a sign-in form until the user pulls a cord, finds a hidden control or completes a game.

rules.title: Give every onboarding step one job and a way back
rules.why: Onboarding completes best when each step is short, predictable and skippable where optional.
do: Keep a back control top-left, Skip top-right on optional steps, a progress bar or dots with an accessible "Step 2 of 4", and one full-width primary button in the same bottom position.
Ask one question per screen, disable Continue until a required choice is made, and keep answers when users go back.
End with a preview of the personalized result and one clear final action.
avoid: Demanding account creation before showing any value when it can be deferred.

rules.title: Show every fee before payment
rules.why: Revealing costs only at the end destroys trust and causes disputes.
do: Number checkout sections on one page, render shipping and payment choices as card-shaped radios with price deltas, and keep a sticky order summary that recalculates instantly.
Before an irreversible payment, show a review sheet listing the amount, each fee and the total, then a processing state, then a confirmation with a copyable reference.
Echo the selected payment method (masked) beside the final button, and collapse the summary into a bar on mobile.
avoid: Fees revealed only after payment, pre-ticked consent to save a card, or double submission while processing.

rules.title: Order product detail panels by the buying decision
rules.why: The buy box should answer what, how much, which variant and when it arrives.
do: Show breadcrumb, name, price with rating and review count, and a short description, then variant radios whose legend names the selection, a quantity stepper and a full-width add button.
Update the total live as options change, show delivery or pickup time near it, and put details, dimensions and care in tabs or accordions below.
avoid: Color-only swatches, stepper buttons under 44x44px, or price changes revealed only at checkout.

rules.title: State price, trial and terms plainly on paywalls
rules.why: Trust and conversion improve when the price, trial length and cancellation terms sit beside the button.
do: Show plan cards with price per period, a clear selected state and a few benefits; name the action and its terms on the button ("Start 7-day free trial").
Put "Cancel anytime, charged after 7 days" and "Restore purchases" under the button, and keep the close control visible.
avoid: Fake countdowns, reappearing "one-time" offers, or a hidden or delayed close button.

rules.title: Make error pages explain and offer a way forward
rules.why: An error page is a dead end unless it says what happened in plain words.
do: Use a small eyebrow with the code, a plain headline ("Page not found"), one sentence of explanation, a primary action home and a secondary "Go back".
On 401 offer sign-in; on 403 explain access and how to request it.
Keep illustrations decorative and below the actions.
avoid: Jokes in place of an explanation, or animated error pages with no navigation.

rules.title: Structure messaging around list, thread and composer
rules.why: Seeing conversations and the open thread together speeds triage.
do: Show conversations with avatar, name, one-line preview, time and an unread badge; highlight the open one.
Align bubbles by sender, pin the composer with labeled attach and send buttons (send disabled while empty), and collapse to one pane with Back on narrow screens.
avoid: Unread or presence shown by a colored dot alone.

rules.title: Keep context visible with bottom sheets
rules.why: A sheet over a map or list holds the current step while the context stays visible and actions stay in thumb reach.
do: Use a sheet with a visible handle and snap points, a short status headline, and the primary action pinned at its bottom.
In live-service flows show ETA, progress and identifying details (name, photo, vehicle) so users can verify the provider, with call, message and cancel actions (cancel confirmed).
For quick-create sheets, name the context in the subtitle and offer equal-width Cancel and Save, dismissible by swipe, Escape or Cancel.
avoid: A primary action that scrolls out of view inside the sheet, or a floating button that covers the last item.

rules.title: Make order confirmations complete and lasting
rules.why: Buyers need to know what they bought, how they paid and when it arrives.
do: Show a success icon, "Order confirmed", the order number, payment method with the last four digits, the items and a delivery tracker.
Offer a secondary action such as "Order another" or "View receipt".
avoid: Confirmation only as a transient animation or toast, or a celebration longer than a second before the details.

rules.title: Order landing pages the way visitors evaluate
rules.why: A familiar section order helps visitors judge a product quickly.
do: Use navigation with one call to action, a hero with one primary action, then features, a short numbered "how it works" (3-4 steps), proof, FAQ, a closing call to action and the footer.
Keep price and the purchase action within the first viewport for single-product pages.
avoid: Burying price and purchase after long storytelling sections.

rules.title: Mask sensitive values on finance screens
rules.why: Balances and card numbers are often viewed in public.
do: Show card numbers as bullets with the last four digits and never the full number on overview screens.
Offer an eye toggle beside balances (aria-pressed, "Hide balance") and remember the choice.
Lead finance home screens with the balance, labeled quick actions and recent activity.
avoid: Icon-only quick actions, or full card number and expiry shown together.

rules.title: Design assistant surfaces around the user's data
rules.why: An assistant is most useful when it shows what it can do and answers next to the data it describes.
do: Offer 2-4 suggestion chips above a composer with a labeled send button, and group history by recency.
Show a live status line while the assistant works, stream replies into a polite live region, and include the period and source for any figure it reports.
Dock the panel beside the data rather than over it, and let users dismiss it.
avoid: Floating orbs or mascots that cover data, or generated figures without their time range.

rules.title: Anchor overlays on immersive views to the corners
rules.why: Overlays on 3D, map or video canvases must leave the center clear and stay readable over moving imagery.
do: Anchor legends, minimaps and live readouts to corners with safe-area insets, on translucent backing plates.
Make legends collapsible and offer on-screen or touch controls alongside keyboard keys.
avoid: Bare text floating on a busy scene, or keyboard-only controls.

rules.title: Commit to one visual style
rules.why: A consistent style gives a product a coherent personality; mixing styles looks unplanned.
do: If a named style is wanted, apply its traits consistently: glass (translucent blurred panels with thin light borders), soft extruded (controls in the background hue shaped by paired light and dark shadows), bold flat (saturated fills, thick dark outlines, hard offset shadows) or flat minimal (solid fills, no depth effects).
Verify contrast for text, controls and focus states in the chosen style.
avoid: Mixing several styles in one product.
rules.note: Translucent and soft-extruded styles often fail contrast for controls and text; check every state.

rules.title: Floating tab bar
rules.why: A floating, rounded tab bar can give a mobile app a distinctive feel while keeping destinations in reach.
do: Inset a fully rounded bar from the screen edges above the safe area, with a soft shadow and 4-5 destinations.
Mark the active tab with a filled icon and label inside a contrasting pill, and keep labels or accessible names on every tab.
Add bottom padding to the scroll container so the bar never hides content.
avoid: Hiding labels on inactive tabs without accessible names, or more than five destinations.

rules.title: Emphasized create action in the tab bar
rules.why: One larger accent button can separate an app's core create action from ordinary navigation.
do: Use it for exactly one action (create post, add entry), with an accessible label.
Prefer a detached floating button at the trailing edge over a slot inside the row of destinations.
avoid: Emphasizing more than one item, or using the emphasized slot for a regular destination.

rules.title: Signature glow button
rules.why: A luminous, layered treatment can make one special action, such as an AI "Generate" button, feel distinct.
do: Build it from consistent layers: a radial gradient fill, a fading 1px highlight stroke, soft inset highlights and tinted drop shadows.
Verify the label meets 4.5:1 against the lightest part of the gradient.
avoid: Using it on more than one action per screen, or heavy blur and blend layers on low-end devices.

rules.title: Translucent blur on floating chrome
rules.why: Blurred translucent bars and inputs over imagery add depth while keeping context visible.
do: Use a translucent fill with backdrop-filter blur, plus a subtle gradient so text stays readable.
Provide a solid fallback for reduce-transparency settings and browsers without backdrop-filter.
avoid: Stacked heavy blurs that cost performance or drop text contrast.

rules.title: Additive glows on dark backgrounds
rules.why: Decorative light effects look natural when they brighten what is beneath them instead of sitting on top as opaque blobs.
do: Build glows from a small bright core and a larger dim halo with an additive blend (mix-blend-mode: plus-lighter or screen).
Keep glows behind content, never behind body text.
avoid: Glows that reduce legibility or cost noticeable rendering time.

rules.title: Glossy showcase icon tile
rules.why: A layered gradient tile with a soft halo and glow gives hero or store artwork depth and polish.
do: Use a square tile with continuous corners at about 24% of its size, a gradient between neighboring hues and a white glyph.
Add a faint, larger halo tile and a blurred same-gradient glow beneath it, built with pseudo-elements and filter: blur().
avoid: Using this treatment for small in-app icons, or many large blur filters on performance-sensitive pages.

rules.title: Tint surfaces with colors from the imagery
rules.why: Echoing a product photo's dominant color in its card gives a cohesive, characterful look.
do: Use a light tint of the image's dominant color for the card background and a darker shade of the same hue for text and icons.
Verify text contrast on the tint.
avoid: Tints strong enough to weaken the product or the text, or this treatment in dense data UI.

rules.title: Atmospheric background imagery
rules.why: A deeply cropped, toned-down image used full-bleed adds mood without adding controls.
do: Crop a high-resolution image until it reads as texture, lower its intensity and blend it with a color layer that matches the palette.
Add an overlay wherever text or a logo sits on top and check contrast.
avoid: Upscaled low-resolution images, or heavy images on pages where load time matters.

rules.title: Overlap elements for depth
rules.why: Slight overlaps, such as an avatar crossing the edge of a cover image, create layering that ties sections together.
do: Let avatars overlap cover images with a ring in the surface color, and use overlapping avatar stacks for groups of people.
avoid: Overlaps that hide content or shrink touch targets.

rules.title: Editorial and calm styles
rules.why: An editorial or calm look comes from scale contrast and restraint, not decoration.
do: Use one grotesk or a serif display face for large titles beside small metadata, a monochrome or warm neutral base and one accent for the active item.
For calm or wellbeing products, slow the pace with short single-sentence steps that still have a Continue button.
avoid: Extra accents and heavy shadows, or steps that auto-advance without user control.

rules.title: Decorative canvas, WebGL and particle effects
rules.why: Particle systems, 3D scenes and simulations are expensive and must never degrade the page or hide content.
do: Cap particle counts, lazy-load 3D libraries, cap devicePixelRatio around 1.5-2 and pause rendering when off-screen or when the tab is hidden.
Keep headlines and navigation as real DOM elements, mark the canvas aria-hidden and provide a static fallback for reduced motion, low-power devices and missing WebGL.
avoid: Unbounded particle arrays, or navigation that depends on exploring a 3D scene.

rules.title: Playful novelty interactions
rules.why: Mascots, physics toys and skeuomorphic gimmicks delight once but slow down repeated tasks.
do: Reserve them for low-frequency moments such as a confirmation or a first visit, keep the underlying control standard, and mark the decoration aria-hidden.
Drive characters from one derived state (for example covering their eyes while the password field is focused) and serve a static pose under reduced motion.
avoid: Delaying focus, typing or submission for an animation, or putting instructions only in a character's speech bubble.

rules.title: Ambient gradient light
rules.why: Soft gradient light behind a hero or form adds atmosphere without image weight.
do: Stack a few radial gradients over a dark base, keep any motion slow and paused under reduced motion, and keep text off the brightest area.
avoid: High-contrast animated backgrounds behind body text.

rules.title: Glass refraction with SVG filters
rules.why: A displacement map bends what is behind a panel, which reads as real glass more convincingly than blur alone.
do: Apply an feDisplacementMap through backdrop-filter: url(#glass) as progressive enhancement over a plain blur fallback, with colorful structure behind the panel.
Keep every safeguard from the translucent-surface contrast rule.
avoid: Relying on url() backdrop filters, which only some engines support, or glass over a flat background.

rules.title: Animate transform and opacity
rules.why: Transform and opacity run on the compositor; animating layout properties forces reflow on every frame.
do: Move, scale and fade with transform and opacity, and fill meters with transform: scaleX() from transform-origin: left.
Use the individual translate, scale and rotate properties when several sources (hover, keyframes, script) animate one element, and give each property one owner.
When a rounded pill must change length without squashing its ends, animate width on that one element with contain: layout style.
avoid: Animating top, left, width or height on many elements, or several sources writing the transform shorthand at once.

rules.title: Keep a duration budget
rules.why: Consistent, short durations keep interfaces responsive; long sequences belong only to rare moments.
do: Use about 100-300ms for micro feedback, 200-450ms for panels, morphs and route changes, and finish staggered entrances within about 600ms.
Keep celebrations under about 1.2s per segment and let users skip them.
Keep the next view usable immediately while decorative motion finishes.
avoid: Multi-second animation on routine actions, or blocking input until an animation ends.

rules.title: Match easing to the motion
rules.why: Easing tells people whether something is arriving, leaving or physical.
do: Use ease-out for entrances and responses, ease-in for exits, and a spring or springy curve (linear() or an overshooting cubic-bezier) only for physical or celebratory moments.
Store easings and durations as tokens and reuse them.
avoid: Bouncy overshoot on navigation people use constantly, or "spring" as a CSS timing keyword (it is not valid).

rules.title: Reduced motion removes decoration, never the state change
rules.why: Vestibular-sensitive users need motion off while still seeing what changed.
do: Wrap travel, parallax, 3D flips, loops and pointer-follow effects in @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference), or check matchMedia in script.
Under reduced motion jump straight to end states, still updating counts, labels and icons, and replace looping loaders with a static indicator plus text.
avoid: Infinite decorative animation with no reduced-motion path, or skipping the state update along with the animation.

rules.title: Pause what nobody can see
rules.why: Animation loops that keep running off-screen or after motion settles waste battery and main-thread time.
do: Start requestAnimationFrame loops on demand and stop them once values settle.
Pause loops when the element is off-screen (IntersectionObserver) or the tab is hidden (visibilitychange).
avoid: Perpetual loops for effects that are idle or invisible.

rules.title: Stagger related entrances briefly
rules.why: A short stagger gives grouped elements a readable order instead of everything popping at once.
do: Offset siblings by about 40-80ms, animating opacity plus a small translate (8-24px) or scale (0.96 to 1), and stagger only the first few items of long lists.
Use animation-fill-mode: backwards on delayed entrances so items wait invisibly instead of flashing.
Keep content visible by default and add the hidden start state only when scripts run and motion is allowed.
avoid: Staggering dozens of items one by one, or content hidden until scripts load.

rules.title: Morph one element instead of crossfading two
rules.why: When the same surface grows into the next state, people keep track of where they are; crossfades create muddy double images.
do: Use the View Transitions API (document.startViewTransition with a shared view-transition-name) or FLIP to grow a button into its panel and shrink it back.
Let the container settle first (about 250-450ms), then fade the inner content (about 150ms), with the anchor fixed at the trigger.
avoid: Scaling text during a morph, stacking two headlines in place, or chaining several morphs without user input.

rules.title: Use FLIP for layout changes
rules.why: Measuring first and animating only transform gives smooth layout transitions without layout thrash.
do: Measure with getBoundingClientRect, apply the change, compute the offset and play element.animate() from the inverted transform back to none.
Measure an untransformed wrapper, because a rotated or scaled element reports its bounding box, not its real size.
Animate new items from where they came from, such as the drop point of an upload.
avoid: Moving elements by animating left, top or width.

rules.title: Move one shared indicator between items
rules.why: A single highlight that glides between options explains a change of selection better than items flashing on and off.
do: Render one indicator (pill, underline or dot) and move it with transform to the active item, about 180-250ms ease-out or a soft spring.
Keep it behind the label so text keeps its contrast, and jump without the slide under reduced motion.
avoid: Re-mounting a separate indicator per item, or animating its left and width every frame.

rules.title: Sequence animations on real completion events
rules.why: Chained guessed timeouts drift out of sync; completion events keep multi-step sequences correct and cancellable.
do: Await element.animate(...).finished, or listen for animationend and transitionend filtered by name, before the next step.
For multi-part scenes, run every part on one shared duration with keyframe percentages, and end state changes from the animation events.
Give each phase a state class or data attribute so it is easy to reverse or skip.
avoid: Nested setTimeout chains or fixed waits that drift from the CSS durations.

rules.title: Register custom properties you animate
rules.why: Unregistered custom properties cannot interpolate, so color and number tweens snap halfway.
do: Declare them with @property (syntax "<number>", "<color>", "<percentage>", with initial-value) and transition or animate them directly.
Drive several visuals (position, shadow, color, glow) from one registered variable with calc() so they stay consistent.
Keep calc() types valid and provide an instant fallback where @property is unsupported.
avoid: Expecting plain custom properties to animate, or type-mismatched calc() that silently drops the whole declaration.

rules.title: Use springs for interruptible physical motion
rules.why: Damped springs feel physical and can be interrupted mid-motion, unlike fixed-duration tweens.
do: Integrate with the frame's delta time (v += (-k * x - c * v) * dt; x += v * dt) and stop when position and velocity fall below a small threshold.
Write spring results into custom properties or transforms, and use CSS linear() spring approximations where a fixed end point is enough.
Keep simple on and off visuals near-instant; springs are for movement.
avoid: Frame-rate-dependent integration without delta time, or long wobbly settles on primary navigation.

rules.title: Move content in the direction of navigation
rules.why: Content that slides the way the user went preserves spatial orientation.
do: Compute the direction from the old and new index and slide the outgoing view out on that side while the next enters from the other.
Overlap the tweens slightly and use a strong ease-out.
avoid: Sliding the same way whether the user went forward or back.

rules.title: Animate changing numbers without jitter
rules.why: Counting to a new value signals fresh data, but changing digit widths make the layout twitch.
do: Tween over about 500-1000ms with ease-out, format each frame with Intl.NumberFormat, and use tabular numerals with a minimum width.
Expose only the final value to assistive technology and show it immediately under reduced motion.
avoid: Counters inside live regions (every frame gets announced), or replaying the count on every visit or re-render.

rules.title: Use clip-path for reveals and shape morphs
rules.why: Clip-path reveals are cheap and can grow a dot into a fill or open a panel from the tap point without layout work.
do: Animate between shapes of the same function (inset to inset, circle to circle) expressed in lengths, for example circle(0 at x y) to circle(150% at x y).
Use negative inset values so focus rings and shadows are not clipped, and keep clipped content out of the focus order until revealed.
avoid: Mixing shape functions, which snaps instead of animating.

rules.title: Treat scroll-driven effects as enhancement
rules.why: Scroll-linked motion can tell a product story, but content must work without it and scrolling must stay native.
do: Use animation-timeline: view() with animation-range where supported, or IntersectionObserver, animating only transform and opacity.
For pinned stages use position: sticky inside a tall section with 100svh height, provide a skip link, and show static images under reduced motion.
avoid: Scroll-jacking, changing scroll speed, or unrevealed text left too faint to read.

rules.title: Never make people wait for decoration
rules.why: Animation that holds back a real result or the next input costs time on every use.
do: Send the request immediately and let any themed animation play alongside it, using a short minimum display time only to avoid flicker.
Keep the actual state change (item in cart, signed in, sent) independent of the animation finishing.
avoid: Artificial delays before network calls, or multi-second sequences in front of frequent actions.

rules.title: Enable pointer-driven effects only for fine pointers
rules.why: Tilt, cursor labels and parallax need a precise pointer and get in the way elsewhere.
do: Enable them only when matchMedia("(hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)") matches, batch updates in requestAnimationFrame, and keep angles small.
Settle the effect while a field inside is focused, and keep the system cursor visible.
avoid: Running these effects on touch devices or under reduced motion.

rules.title: Make long-running motion pausable
rules.why: Anything that moves for more than five seconds alongside other content must be stoppable.
do: Give marquees, autoplaying video and looping backgrounds a pause control, pause on hover and focus, and stop them under reduced motion.
Autoplay video only muted, with playsinline and a poster image.
avoid: Unmuted autoplay, or essential information only inside a moving ticker.

rules.title: Split text for animation without breaking screen readers
rules.why: Wrapping each word or letter in an element makes screen readers spell text out unless the full string is preserved.
do: Put the full text in an aria-label on the container and aria-hidden on the generated spans.
Animate words and letters with separate wrappers so transforms do not overwrite each other, and limit split animation to short headlines.
avoid: Per-letter animation on body copy, or split spans exposed to assistive technology.

rules.title: Start from native elements
rules.why: Native elements bring focus, keyboard activation, form behavior and correct announcements for free.
do: Use button type="button" for actions, a href for navigation, mailto links and downloads (a download), and a real form with a submit button.
Check that forms work unstyled and without scripts, then layer validation and animation on top, adding novalidate only when your script replaces native messages.
avoid: Div click handlers, or role="button" without tabindex and key handling.

rules.title: Model async controls as a state machine
rules.why: Download, pay, send and add buttons have mutually exclusive states; independent flags allow impossible combinations and double submissions.
do: Declare the allowed transitions (idle to working to done or failed, and back) and reflect the current state in one data-state attribute that all styling reads.
Ignore activation unless the state allows it, set aria-busy and disabled or aria-disabled while working, and auto-reset after a short confirmation when the action repeats.
avoid: Separate loading, success and error booleans that can all be true, or a second click restarting the request mid-flight.

rules.title: Keep button size stable across label changes
rules.why: Swapping "Pay" for "Done" changes width and shifts the layout under the pointer.
do: Render every state label in the same grid cell (display: grid with each label at grid-area: 1 / 1) and show the active one with visibility, so the widest sets the size.
Hide inactive labels from assistive technology and announce the new state in a live region; keep icon-only phases named (aria-label="Pay $248.00").
avoid: Replacing the label text and letting the button resize, or exposing all stacked labels to screen readers at once.

rules.title: Keep the hit box still and animate an inner layer
rules.why: If the element receiving pointer events moves, hover flickers and clicks miss.
do: Give the outer link or button a fixed box and apply transforms to an inner span, driving state from a data attribute set on pointerenter and pointerleave.
avoid: Scaling or translating the element that receives pointer events.

rules.title: Make hidden and covered content inert
rules.why: Content that is visually hidden or covered must not take focus or be read out.
do: Set inert on inactive panes, covered forms and non-current wizard steps, switching it at the moment content is fully covered, then move focus to the first field of the new view.
Make the page behind an open dialog or sheet inert, and restore focus to the trigger on close.
avoid: Visually hidden but focusable fields, or aria-hidden on containers that hold focusable controls.

rules.title: Drive one root state attribute
rules.why: One state on the component root keeps visuals, tokens and semantics in sync.
do: Toggle a single class or data attribute on the root and style descendants from it.
Update inert and aria attributes in the same function that changes the state.
avoid: Scattered per-element flags that can contradict each other.

rules.title: Render repeated UI from data and format at render time
rules.why: Defining tiles, rows and menus as data keeps markup consistent and values computable.
do: Map arrays of raw values ({ title, value, change, icon }) to one component with stable keys.
Store numbers and dates raw and format them at render with Intl.NumberFormat and Intl.DateTimeFormat.
avoid: Copy-pasted near-identical markup per item, or preformatted strings that cannot be sorted or summed.

rules.title: Enhance heavy visuals progressively
rules.why: Canvas, WebGL and animation libraries can fail or load late; the interface must stay usable and themable without them.
do: Ship a CSS or static fallback and remove it only after the enhanced version has painted.
Keep colors and sizes in CSS custom properties and read them from script with getComputedStyle.
Lazy-load heavy libraries and show loading progress for large assets.
avoid: Hard-coded colors and sizes in script, or a selected state that disappears when scripts fail.

rules.title: Schedule clocks and countdowns against real time
rules.why: Interval timers drift; scheduling against the wall clock keeps displays accurate.
do: Schedule each tick for the next whole second (1000 - Date.now() % 1000 ms) and read the time again from Date.
Render times in a time element with tabular numerals and keep rotating hands moving forward.
Announce only meaningful thresholds, never every tick.
avoid: setInterval counting its own ticks, or a live region on a clock that changes every second.

rules.title: Persist interface preferences safely
rules.why: Theme, sidebar, sound and similar choices should survive reloads without breaking when storage is unavailable.
do: Store small preferences in localStorage wrapped in try/catch and fall back to defaults when it fails.
Read system preferences (prefers-color-scheme, prefers-reduced-motion) for first-run defaults.
avoid: Crashing or blocking rendering when storage is blocked.

rules.title: Package reusable widgets as custom elements
rules.why: A custom element configured by attributes drops into any stack without a build step.
do: Register the element as a module, configure it through attributes, reflect its state on the host and style states with :host([state="done"]).
avoid: Shipping test-only attributes (such as simulated progress) without a real progress source.

rules.title: Match system chrome to the theme and clean up listeners
rules.why: Status-bar colors, orientation locks and leaked listeners cause flashes, jank and memory leaks in apps.
do: Initialize the shell before the first frame (preload assets, set transparent system bars with icon brightness from the active theme).
Lock orientation only when the layout truly cannot adapt, and dispose controllers, listeners and subscriptions when screens close.
avoid: Hard-coded dark status-bar icons in both themes, or listeners left running after a screen is gone.

rules.title: Test the flows users depend on
rules.why: Automated flow tests catch regressions in the screens people use most.
do: Write integration or end-to-end tests that launch the app, walk the main paths (browse, detail, checkout; sign in, verify) and assert visible text and states.
Cover the failure path (wrong code, declined payment) as well as success.
avoid: Relying only on manual tapping in a simulator.

rules.title: Build the mark on a grid and document clear space
rules.why: A documented construction and exclusion zone keeps the mark consistent from billboards to favicons.
do: Construct the symbol and wordmark from simple geometry on guides for baseline, cap height and shared stroke widths.
Define clear space as a multiple of a mark element, a minimum size, and lockups: symbol plus wordmark, symbol only, and a reversed version for photos and saturated backgrounds.
avoid: Stretching, recoloring or crowding the mark, or placing it on busy photography without a scrim.

rules.title: Design app icons for small sizes
rules.why: An icon must stay recognizable beside other icons, on any wallpaper and at tiny sizes.
do: Center one bold symbol at roughly 55-65% of the icon width on a solid background with strong figure-ground contrast.
Preview it at home-screen and settings sizes beside common icons on light, dark and photo wallpapers, and check monochrome and tinted variants.
avoid: Full wordmarks, thin strokes or fine detail inside the icon, or gradients that turn muddy when small.

rules.title: Document the palette with roles, values and approved pairs
rules.why: A named palette with roles keeps color consistent across print, web and product.
do: Give each color a name, HEX and RGB values and a role (background, text, accent, secondary), and expose them as design tokens in code.
Record which text-on-color pairs are approved, with their contrast ratios.
Prefer a soft near-black over pure black for brand dark.
avoid: Small white text on mid-tone brand colors, or palette value labels printed in near-invisible tints.

rules.title: Apply the identity the same way everywhere
rules.why: Recognition comes from a few rules repeated on every touchpoint.
do: Reuse the same symbol, palette tokens, typeface and image treatment across the product, website, social profiles, print and merchandise.
Carry a signature product element into marketing mockups so product and brand match.
avoid: New accent colors, logo variants or image treatments per channel.

rules.title: Write tone of voice as positions on scales
rules.why: Placing the voice on a few spectra gives writers a concrete target for interface copy.
do: Define 3-5 scales (funny to serious, formal to casual, enthusiastic to matter-of-fact) and mark the brand's position on each.
Translate positions into concrete copy rules with examples, such as warm but precise for money and no jokes in payment errors.
avoid: Voice described only as vague adjectives with no examples.
